title: Dining Hall: Small Talk Starter
summary: Practice low-stakes social exposure in the dining hall. Navigate entering crowded spaces, asking simple questions, and tolerating brief social moments.
author: HeyPsych Clinical Content Team
learningObjectives: Practice entering crowded social spaces despite anxiety
Ask simple direct questions like 'is this seat taken?'
Interpret neutral responses as normal, not negative
Build tolerance for brief social moments

nodes.text:
You push through the heavy doors. The dining hall hits you all at once—clattering trays, overlapping conversations, clusters of people everywhere. Your chest tightens. Everyone looks like they belong here. You spot the food line and a few scattered empty tables.

What do you do?

You take a breath and sketch a quick mental plan: get food, find a seat, eat. Simple. The anxiety doesn't vanish, but having a micro-plan helps. You join the line.

Standing in line, you're hyper-aware of people around you. Are they looking at you? Probably not. But your mind whispers 'you look awkward just standing here.'

What do you do?

You pull out your phone and scroll. It's a familiar safety move—something to do with your hands, a reason not to make eye contact. The anxiety dulls slightly, but you also feel... hidden. You get your food.

Now you're holding a tray, scanning for a seat. There are a few options.

What do you do?

You turn around before even getting in line. The noise, the crowd, the feeling of being watched—it's too much right now. You leave, and relief floods in as you exit.

As you walk away, your inner critic pipes up. But that voice isn't the whole story.

An hour later, your stomach growls. You're hungry. The dining hall is still open.

You hold your tray and scan the room. There's an empty table in the corner—safe, quiet. There's also a table with one person sitting alone, reading. And a bigger table with a few open seats near a group chatting.

Your anxiety spikes. Where do you sit?

You walk toward the table with a few people. Your heart pounds. This is the moment. You stop near an empty chair.

You clear your throat slightly and ask: 'Is this seat taken?'

The person nearest you glances up. 'Nope, go ahead,' they say, then return to their conversation.

Neutral. Not warm, not cold. Just... normal.

What do you do?

You head to the empty corner table. Sitting alone feels safer. You eat quickly, earbuds in, eyes down. The anxiety is manageable—you made it through.

But as you finish, you notice other people at tables, talking, laughing. Part of you wonders what it would be like to try.

You stayed. That's something.

You sit down. After a moment, you try something small: 'How's your day going?'

The person looks up again, a bit surprised but not annoyed. 'Pretty good, thanks. You?'

'Not bad,' you say. They nod and go back to their food.

It wasn't deep. It wasn't perfect. But you did it—a real, brief, normal social moment.

You eat your meal. The anxiety fades slightly. You stayed, you asked, you connected for a second.

You sit down and focus on your food. You don't say anything else. The brief interaction was enough—maybe more than enough. Your phone sits next to your tray, a quiet shield.

You made it. You asked the question, you sat near people. That's progress, even if you didn't push further.

They said 'go ahead,' but their tone felt... flat. Were they annoyed? Did you interrupt? Your mind races. Maybe they didn't want you there. The spotlight feeling intensifies.

You sit, but the meal feels uncomfortable. You eat quickly and leave.

You tried. But the mind-reading pulled you back into avoidance mode.

endings.title: Confident Step
endings.text:
You did it. You walked into a crowded dining hall, asked a direct question, and even tried a brief follow-up. It wasn't perfect—it never is—but you stayed present despite the anxiety.

This is what small reps look like: uncomfortable, brief, real. You're building the skill of showing up even when the spotlight feeling is loud.

Next time will still be hard. But you proved you can do hard things.

endings.title: Mixed But Moving
endings.text:
You made it through. You entered the dining hall, got food, and sat down. Maybe you used your phone as a shield, or chose the corner table, or didn't push for more interaction.

That's okay. You didn't bail completely. You stayed in the space, even if it felt uncomfortable.

Progress isn't always a straight line. Sometimes just showing up is the rep.

endings.title: Avoidance Loop
endings.text:
You left before giving yourself a chance. The relief was instant—walking away always is—but it came with a cost. Avoidance teaches your brain that the dining hall is dangerous, that you can't handle it.

The truth? You probably could have. But avoidance doesn't let you find out.

Next time, try staying just one minute longer. The discomfort won't kill you—but avoiding it keeps the fear alive.
